title: The Tribunal and the Paraclete: a Carthaginian Lawyer's Case Against the Empire and Then Against His Own Church
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Carthage, birth in Africa Proconsularis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source gives a birth year, month, parents or household; c. 155-160 is the conventional estimate and c. 150-170 the defensible range [R, Barnes, Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study, via tertullian.org/chronology.htm]. The birthplace rests on Jerome's testimony alone, not on anything Tertullian says of himself [A, Jerome, De viris illustribus 53].
stops.campa: A son is born at Carthage, capital of Africa Proconsularis, in a century that keeps no register of him. No year survives, no month, no parents, no house. Jerome supplies the city more than a hundred and seventy years later, and everything else in the traditional account of the childhood is inference drawn back out of the Latin the man would eventually write. Scholars place the birth around 155 to 160 and will defend anything from 150 to 170. The city is the one solid thing: after Rome the largest and wealthiest in the Latin West, with courts and temples and baths and schools of rhetoric working under the Byrsa hill.
suggested_refs: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53, the sole ancient authority for the Carthaginian birth
sources: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53, at tertullian.org/jerome_biog.htm
Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study (1971, rev. 1985)

stops.name: Carthage, the harbour and the working city
stops.date_confidence: undated civic backdrop, placed here only to order the segment. The description of Roman Carthage is uncontroversial [A, Serge Lancel, Carthage: A History]; the harbour coordinate is approximate and was not verified against a cited source by the research pool [R].
stops.campa: Below the Byrsa the double harbour of the old Punic city still takes shipping, the circular cothon that once held war galleys now working grain and oil for Rome. A boy raised here learns an empire by watching it unload. He will write about all of it later with the accuracy of somebody who has been inside, and he never explains how he came to know. Everything he condemns stands within a morning's walk of this water: the theatre, the circus, the amphitheatre, the temples of the imperial cult, the baths where a province conducts its leisure.
suggested_refs: The Punic circular harbour (cothon) at Carthage, still in use under Rome
sources: Serge Lancel, Carthage: A History (1995 Eng. tr.)

stops.name: Forum of Carthage, the training in forensic Latin
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, undated. No teacher, school or lawsuit is named in any surviving source; the education is inferred from the writing itself [R]. The research pool tagged this claim A in its chronology and R in its geography, and flagged the two entries as inconsistent with each other; the R reading is followed here.
stops.campa: The Latin is the evidence. It moves in the forms of the courts: praescriptio, actio, the burden of proof, the objection raised before the case is heard, and behind those a reading of Virgil, Cicero, Seneca, the Stoics, and enough Greek to argue with Greeks. No teacher is named. No school is named. No case is recorded in which he stands and pleads. The forum of a provincial capital is where such training was had, so the training is placed here on the strength of the prose and nothing else. What the prose cannot supply is a single day of it.
suggested_refs: The legal vocabulary of the corpus, catalogued at tertullian.org/works.htm
sources: Internal evidence of Tertullian's surviving corpus (tertullian.org/works.htm)
Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study

stops.name: Governor's tribunal, Carthage: the Scillitan twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day [A, Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs, the earliest precisely dated Latin Christian document]. No source ties Tertullian personally to this trial; it is included as documented civic background, not as an event in his life.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of July, twelve Christians from Scilli stand before the proconsul Publius Vigellius Saturninus. He offers them thirty days to think again. They refuse, and the sentence is decapitation. The record of the hearing survives as a transcript, question and answer, with no rhetoric anywhere in it, and it is the earliest precisely dated Christian document in Latin. The church Tertullian will speak for twenty years later is already in this city, already being killed, already keeping its own minutes. Nothing places him in that crowd.
suggested_refs: Acta Martyrum Scillitanorum, the transcript of the 17 July 180 hearing
sources: Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs, trans. at livius.org/sources/content/acts-of-the-scillitan-martyrs/translation/

segments.name: The Wife, the Water, and a Career He May Never Have Had

stops.name: Carthage, the wife with no name
stops.date_confidence: undated. The marriage is attested only by the treatise addressed to her [A, Ad uxorem]; no name, wedding date, children or later history survives, and whether the marriage preceded or followed his conversion is unknown [R for the ordering date].
stops.campa: Two books survive addressed to his wife. She is never named, and the marriage has no date, no dowry, no children on record, no later history. In the first he asks her, if he dies before her, not to marry again; in the second he concedes that if she must, she should marry only in the Lord. He reasons at her in the second person, at length, about her own widowhood, while he is still alive to do it. She is the clearest fact anyone has about his private life and she is entirely a silhouette. Nothing else about her survives.
stops.quote: The precept, therefore, which I give you is, that, with all the constancy you may, you do, after our departure, renounce nuptials.
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, Ad uxorem I.1 (ANF tr.), newadvent.org/fathers/0404.htm
suggested_refs: Ad uxorem, two books addressed to an unnamed Christian wife
sources: Tertullian, Ad uxorem I.1 and II.2 (ANF tr.), newadvent.org/fathers/0404.htm

stops.name: Carthage, the conversion nobody wrote down
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. c. 193-196 is scholarly convention, derived from the internal dating of the earliest works rather than from any account of the event [R, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]. No font, baptizer, church, day or motive is recorded.
stops.campa: He becomes a Christian at some point before the first book anyone can date. There is no font, no bishop, no day, no witness, no account in his own hand of what changed. The popular story, that the courage of the martyrs under the sword converted him, is read backward out of a sentence in the Apologeticum by later biographers who wanted a scene. He supplies none, then or afterward, in thirty surviving treatises. What can be said is that a man trained to argue in the courts of the empire stands on one side of a line in the early 190s and on the other side by 197.
suggested_refs: Apologeticum 50, the passage from which the martyr-conversion story was later inferred
sources: Tertullian, Ad nationes and Apologeticum, internal dating

stops.name: Roman Forum, the jurist who is probably not him
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition, pinned here to place the legend rather than the man. Eusebius's description is attested [A, Historia Ecclesiastica II.2, written early 4th c.]; the identification of the theologian with the jurist Tertullianus excerpted in Justinian's Digest of 533 is rejected as unproven or improbable by Barnes and Rankin [R]. No source places Tertullian in Rome at any point.
stops.campa: Eusebius calls him a man versed in the laws of the Romans and distinguished at Rome, and on that one sentence a second career was built: Tertullian the jurist, practising in the capital, his opinions excerpted three centuries later in the Digest that Justinian's commissioners closed against commentary. A jurist named Tertullianus is indeed quoted there. Nothing links the two men except a name and a taste for legal vocabulary. Barnes and Rankin regard the identification as broken, and no ancient source puts the Christian of Carthage in Italy at all.
suggested_refs: The excerpts of the jurist Tertullianus in Justinian's Digest, book and title unverified here
sources: Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian; David Rankin, Tertullian and the Church (1995)

segments.name: The First Books: a Brief Filed From a Province

stops.name: Prison, Carthage: the letter into the cells
stops.date_confidence: attested work, conventionally dated before 197 and just ahead of the Apologeticum [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]. The prisoners are unnamed, the prison's location within the city is unrecorded, and the year is a convention rather than a record.
stops.campa: The first thing he writes that anyone can date is a letter into a jail. Christians are being held in Carthage awaiting a hearing that will probably kill them, and he sends them a text arguing that the prison is the better world: outside it the whole province is the real dungeon, darker, and full of idols. He is not in the cell. He tells the prisoners that their keepers feed them and the church supplies them, and that what they endure is training, the way an athlete is shut away from wine and comfort before the contest. Their names are not recorded.
suggested_refs: Ad martyras, addressed to Christians imprisoned at Carthage
sources: Tertullian, Ad martyras (ANF vol. 3, tr. S. Thelwall)

stops.name: Carthage, Ad nationes and a battle already over
stops.date_confidence: attested terminus post quem. Ad nationes refers to Severus's defeat of Clodius Albinus as past, which dates the work after 19 February 197 [A, internal reference, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]. The date given is the battle, not the day of writing.
stops.campa: Septimius Severus destroys Clodius Albinus, his last rival, in February. Tertullian writes Ad nationes with that victory behind him, which is how the book gets its date: two books against the pagans, arguing that Christians are hated on hearsay, tried for a name, and convicted of crimes nobody has troubled to demonstrate. It is a draft in the strict sense. Within months he takes the same material apart and rebuilds it into the Apologeticum, the second time addressing it to the men on the bench rather than to the pagans at large. Ad nationes survives as the working version.
suggested_refs: Ad nationes, the earlier and rougher version of the Apologeticum's argument
sources: Tertullian, Ad nationes, internal reference dated at tertullian.org/chronology.htm

stops.name: Governor's tribunal, the Apologeticum addressed to the bench
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, conventionally later in 197 after the Ad nationes reference to Severus's victory [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; month assigned only to order the segment. It is a literary address, not a brief filed in a known case, and no record shows a governor received or answered it.
stops.campa: He writes it as a brief and addresses it to the bench. The argument is procedural before it is theological. Christians alone are punished for a name without inquiry into the acts the name is supposed to cover; torture is used everywhere else to extract confession and here to extract denial; the law is being run backward. He grants that Christians will pray for the emperor and will not sacrifice to him, and asks the court to notice that these are two different things. No governor is recorded as answering.
stops.quote: Rulers of the Roman Empire, if, seated for the administration of justice on your lofty tribunal...
suggested_refs: Apologeticum, addressed to the provincial governors of the Roman Empire

stops.name: Carthage, the charges turned around
stops.date_confidence: attested content of the Apologeticum [A, newadvent.org/fathers/0301.htm]; the month is an ordering device within 197. These passages are evidence of polemical strategy, not a statistical account of Roman behaviour.
stops.campa: The province says Christians eat infants at their meetings and couple in the dark with their own relatives. He answers by inventory: Roman fathers expose newborns on the roadside, the arena drinks blood by public subscription, and the gods of the theatre commit in myth every incest the accusation imagines. The reversal is the method of a man trained to cross-examine, and it is not a census of how Romans behave. The accusers have never been inside a Christian meeting. The accused have all seen Carthage.
stops.quote: We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.
suggested_refs: Apologeticum, the chapters answering the charges of infanticide and incest

stops.name: Carthage, the sentence that outlived the book
stops.date_confidence: attested text [A, Apologeticum 50.13, Latin and ANF translation]; the month is an ordering device. The familiar English form, the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church, is a later paraphrase and is not in the Latin, which names neither martyrs nor Church.
stops.campa: At the close of the Apologeticum he tells the magistrates that their sentences are agricultural. Executions in the forum are the recruitment of the church; the more efficiently the province kills, the faster the thing it is killing spreads. The version the centuries kept, the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church, adds both the martyrs and the Church to a line that names neither of them, and it is the version that travelled. His own runs to five words: semen est sanguis Christianorum.
stops.quote: The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, Apologeticum 50 (ANF vol. 3, tr. S. Thelwall), ccel.org/ccel/schaff/anf03.iv.iii.l.html
suggested_refs: Apologeticum 50.13, and the later history of its paraphrase

stops.name: Carthage, the soul called as a witness
stops.date_confidence: attested work, dated c. 197-198 by convention [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: A short book with a single device: he calls the soul as a witness and refuses it any education. Not the soul of the schools, he says, not the soul that has read Plato, but the ordinary one that says God is great and God will judge without ever having been taught to. The testimony is common speech itself. He treats the involuntary phrase as evidence and enters it as a deposition. The witness he wants is a Carthaginian saying God bless you in the street, in the same mouth that will sacrifice at a temple that afternoon.
suggested_refs: De testimonio animae, the argument from spontaneous speech
sources: Tertullian, De testimonio animae, dated c. 197-198 at tertullian.org/chronology.htm

segments.name: Athens and Jerusalem: the Rule, the Water, and the Arena

stops.name: Carthage, the objection raised before the case
stops.date_confidence: attested work, assigned to the c. 198-203 cluster [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the year is the middle of that range and the day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: De praescriptione haereticorum takes a Roman courtroom instrument and turns it on doctrine. Praescriptio is the plea that stops a suit before its merits are argued: the plaintiff has no standing to bring this action. So with the Scriptures. Groups he classes as heretics may not argue from a book that belongs to the churches which can name their line back to the apostles. Chapter seven asks what Athens has to do with Jerusalem, a line quoted ever since as a rejection of reason by readers who do not notice that the argument around it is built out of Stoic logic.
stops.quote: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church?
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, De praescriptione haereticorum 7 (ANF tr. Peter Holmes), newadvent.org/fathers/0311.htm
suggested_refs: De praescriptione haereticorum, the transfer of a legal plea into theology

stops.name: Rome, the two graves the rule rests on
stops.date_confidence: ordering date only, inside the c. 198-203 cluster of De praescriptione. That chapter 36 grounds Rome's authority in the deaths of Peter and Paul is [R]: the research pool inferred it from standard scholarship and did not refetch the primary text. That no source places Tertullian himself in Rome, Greece or Asia Minor is [A] as a negative finding across the consulted sources.
stops.campa: The rule needs a place where the line can be shown, and he points at Rome: the church there can produce its succession, and it can produce two deaths. Peter is crucified in the manner of his master; Paul, a citizen, is taken outside and beheaded. Tertullian has not seen the city. Nothing in his own writing or in any ancient source places him in Italy at any point in his life. He reaches Rome the way a provincial lawyer reaches a precedent, by citation, and enters the apostles' executions there as the deed of title for an argument he is making in Carthage.
suggested_refs: De praescriptione haereticorum 36, on the apostolic churches and the Roman succession
sources: Tertullian, De praescriptione haereticorum 36 (attribution inferred, not refetched)
Negative finding on Tertullian's travel, tertullian.org and the dossier's Rome and travel review

stops.name: Carthage, the earliest Latin book on baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested work, assigned to the c. 198-203 cluster [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The earliest surviving Latin treatise on baptism is written to settle a local dispute and settles several others on the way past. Water is not a poor sign of grace but the element God moved on first. Delay the baptism of small children, he says, and of the unmarried, because sin after the water is the graver danger; the argument assumes, as it disapproves, that infant baptism is already being asked for in his city. Women may not teach and may not baptize, whatever the Acts of Paul and Thecla are being made to authorize.
stops.quote: If the writings which wrongly go under Paul's name, claim Thecla's example as a licence for women's teaching and baptizing... Let them be silent, he says, and at home consult their own husbands.
suggested_refs: De baptismo, the first Latin treatise devoted to the rite

stops.name: Carthage, the address to the women of the church
stops.date_confidence: attested text, disputed date: variously placed before c. 197 or in the c. 198-203 cluster [A for the text, R for the year, which is assigned here only to order the segment].
stops.campa: He addresses the Christian women of the city collectively, in the second person, and opens by telling them what they are. Eve's sentence runs in each of them; the dress that follows should be mourning, not ornament. That opening has done more to fix his reputation than anything else he wrote, and the other line everybody attributes to him, the temple built over a sewer, is nowhere in his surviving works. Out go the cosmetics, the dyed hair, the gold, the pearls that cost a fortune and drown in a shipwreck like anything else.
stops.quote: You are the devil's gateway: you are the unsealer of that (forbidden) tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law.
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, De cultu feminarum I.1 (ANF tr.), newadvent.org/fathers/0402.htm
suggested_refs: De cultu feminarum, two books on women's dress and ornament
sources: Tertullian, De cultu feminarum I.1, newadvent.org/fathers/0402.htm
Dossier note: the sewer quotation is not securely located in the extant corpus

stops.name: Carthage, the treatise on patience
stops.date_confidence: attested text [A, De patientia 1, ANF tr.]; the date is an ordering device only, since the treatise carries no secure position in the chronology.
stops.campa: He opens a treatise on patience by admitting he has none. The confession is a rhetorical move, the sick man praising health; it is also the only sentence in thirty treatises where he describes his own temperament, and nothing else he wrote tells anyone what he was like. He goes on to argue that patience is God's own property before it is a virtue of ours, exhibited in the sun that rises on the unjust, in the rain that falls without asking who owns the field, and in Christ standing silent under examination in a court. The philosophers, he adds, keep the word and lose the thing.
stops.quote: So I, most miserable, ever sick with the heats of impatience, must of necessity sigh after, and invoke, and persistently plead for, that health of patience which I possess not.
suggested_refs: De patientia, opening chapter

stops.name: Amphitheatre of Carthage, the seats forbidden
stops.date_confidence: attested work, dated c. 198-206 [A, De spectaculis, ANF vol. 3, newadvent.org/fathers/0303.htm]; the year within that span is an ordering choice. Coordinate corrected during verification to the amphitheatre's actual site west of the Byrsa, 36.85612 N / 10.315078 E, replacing a pool value about 1.2 km out toward the shore.
stops.campa: The amphitheatre stands on flat ground west of the Byrsa, and he forbids his people to enter it, or the theatre, or the circus, or the stadium. The games are idolatry at the root and passion in operation; a Christian sitting in the tiers is worshipping whether he means to or not. Then chapter thirty. He imagines the last judgement as the better spectacle: governors who burned Christians liquefying in fire, tragedians louder than they ever were on stage, charioteers glowing on their wheels. The grammar is the arena's own, turned around and kept. He puts himself in the tiers he has just forbidden, watching.
suggested_refs: De spectaculis 30, the Last Judgement imagined as a spectacle

stops.name: Amphitheatre of Carthage, Perpetua and Felicity
stops.date_confidence: the martyrdom at Carthage in 203, at military games for the birthday of Caesar Geta, is attested [A, Passio Perpetuae; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetua_and_Felicity]. The day, 7 March, is the martyrological feast date and is not stated in the Passio [R]. Tertullian's long-proposed editorship is no longer regarded as established, and no personal meeting is documented.
stops.campa: Vibia Perpetua, a young woman of good family with a child at the breast, and Felicity, her slave, are killed in this amphitheatre with Revocatus, Saturninus, Secundulus and Saturus, at military games for the birthday of the Caesar Geta. For centuries the editor who framed the account was said to be Tertullian, on the strength of shared interests in visions, the Spirit and rigour; modern textual scholarship no longer holds that, and no source records that he ever met her. Inside the account is her own prison diary, one of the earliest texts by a Christian woman in her own hand.
suggested_refs: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, now catalogued as anonymous

stops.name: Carthage, the debate with a Jewish proselyte
stops.date_confidence: attested work, date disputed within his career [R for the year, assigned only to order the segment]. Whether the second half is authentic, unfinished or composite is unresolved; Geoffrey D. Dunn defends the work's rhetorical unity against older doubts. The staged dispute is of contested historicity.
stops.campa: The book opens on a scene: a dispute at Carthage between a Christian and a Jewish proselyte, running all day, ending with nothing settled and the crowd unsatisfied. Whether that debate ever happened is not knowable. What follows argues that the law's observances were given for a season and that the promises pass to the nations. Chapters nine to fourteen overlap the third book against Marcion so closely that scholars have argued for a century that the second half is not his; others read the whole as one deliberate composition. Carthage had a Jewish community. No interlocutor is named.
suggested_refs: Geoffrey D. Dunn, Tertullian's Adversus Iudaeos (2008)
sources: Geoffrey D. Dunn, Tertullian's Adversus Iudaeos (2008)

stops.name: Pepouza, Phrygia: where the New Prophecy begins
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The movement's mid-second-century Phrygian origin is standard scholarship [R, Tabbernee, Trevett]; the exact year is an ordering device. The Pepouza site itself is a modern archaeological identification by Tabbernee and Lampe, near Karayakuplu in the Karahalli district of Usak province; the coordinate was corrected during verification and an erroneous reference to Suhut removed. No text places Tertullian in Phrygia or in the company of Montanus, Prisca or Maximilla.
stops.campa: In upland Phrygia, a generation before he begins to defend it, a man named Montanus and two women, Prisca and Maximilla, begin to speak in the first person as the Paraclete. The movement they start keeps prophecy open: the Spirit did not stop talking when the last apostle died. It fasts harder than the churches around it, forbids remarriage, and forbids running from persecution. Pepouza is its centre, a site archaeologists place in the canyons of what is now Usak province. A generation later, in Carthage, Tertullian will quote all three of them by name. No text puts him in Phrygia.
suggested_refs: William Tabbernee and Peter Lampe's excavation of the Pepouza site

stops.name: Carthage, the lost book on ecstasy
stops.date_confidence: attested as a lost work by ancient testimony (Jerome, De viris illustribus 53; Praedestinatus) [A]; tertullian.org/chronology.htm places the Montanist-leaning group after 204. The year is an ordering choice. No text records a formal joining, an excommunication, or any self-description as a Montanist.
stops.campa: He writes a book in defence of prophetic ecstasy, in several volumes, and it is gone. So are De spe fidelium and De paradiso. What survives is the shift visible in the books that did come through: the Paraclete cited as an authority, the prophets of Phrygia quoted with approval, and the Christians who will not fast as hard as he does acquiring a name in his prose. He calls them psychici, the soulish ones, the merely animal, as against the spiritual. There is no ceremony of joining anywhere on record, and no excommunication either.
suggested_refs: De ecstasi, De spe fidelium and De paradiso, all lost
sources: Clavis Patrum Latinorum, lists of lost works

stops.name: Carthage, the third assault on Marcion
stops.date_confidence: attested by internal reference to the fifteenth year of Severus, giving 207-208 [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]. Tertullian states this is his third version; an earlier draft was stolen and circulated uncorrected. Marcion's own Roman base is named in the campa but is not a place Tertullian is attested to have gone.
stops.campa: Five books, the longest thing he ever finished, and the third attempt: the first draft too hasty, the second stolen by an apostate who put it into circulation uncorrected, and this one dated by its own reference to the fifteenth year of Severus. From Rome, Marcion had taught that the creator of the Hebrew scriptures is not the Father of Jesus, and had cut a Bible down to fit the distinction. Tertullian argues the two testaments back together, one God and one economy, against a man he can neither meet nor persuade. Marcion has been dead some fifty years.
suggested_refs: Ernest Evans, ed., Adversus Marcionem (Oxford, 1972)
sources: Tertullian, Adversus Marcionem (ANF vol. 3, tr. Peter Holmes)

stops.name: Carthage, the soul as a body and the sister who sees
stops.date_confidence: attested work, dated c. 208-212 [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the year is the middle of that range. The research pool could not retrieve the text of De anima 9 directly and relied on the standard critical understanding of the treatise, including J. H. Waszink's edition [R for the chapter reference].
stops.campa: He surveys what the philosophers and the physicians have said about the soul and comes down on the Stoic side: the soul is a body, subtle, with outline and limit, and it is passed from parent to child with the flesh rather than made new at each birth. His evidence includes a woman of his own congregation who receives visions during the service and reports afterward, among other things, having seen a soul in bodily form. He writes down what she saw and uses it to confirm what he already thinks. She is not named.
suggested_refs: De anima 9, on the visionary sister of the Carthage congregation
sources: J. H. Waszink, ed., De anima

stops.name: Carthage, the flesh that is not an appearance
stops.date_confidence: attested text, dated c. 206-212 [A, De carne Christi 5, tr. Ernest Evans]; the month is an ordering device. The maxim credo quia absurdum is not Tertullian's: it was reworded by Thomas Browne in 1643 and recast by Voltaire in 1767, who attributed his own version to Augustine [A, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credo_quia_absurdum; Peter Harrison's scholarship].
stops.campa: Against those who say Christ's flesh was an appearance, he insists on the whole indignity: a real womb, a real birth, a real death, a real burial. The argument turns on shame. What is unworthy of God is exactly what God chose, and the unworthiness is the reason to credit it. Fourteen centuries later Thomas Browne rewords the sentence, and Voltaire recasts it as credo quia absurdum and attributes his own version to Augustine rather than to its author. Tertullian never wrote those three words. He wrote that it is credible because it is inept, and certain because it is impossible.
stops.quote: The Son of God died: it is immediately credible, because it is silly. He was buried, and rose again: it is certain, because it is impossible.
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, De carne Christi 5, tr. Ernest Evans, tertullian.org/works/de_carne_christi.htm
suggested_refs: Peter Harrison, on the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century manufacture of credo quia absurdum

stops.name: A camp in Africa Proconsularis, the crown refused
stops.date_confidence: attested work and scene [A, De corona 1, ANF tr., newadvent.org/fathers/0304.htm], dated c. 211. The camp is not named in the text; the coordinate is a generic African placement given Tertullian's vantage, and the incident could have occurred anywhere in the empire. The soldier is unnamed.
stops.campa: A donative is distributed in camp and the men come up garlanded. One soldier walks with his head bare and the laurel in his hand. The tribune asks why he alone is out of step; he answers that he is a Christian; the belt comes off, the heavy shoes and the sword go down, and he is held to wait for a sentence. Other Christians in the camp call him rash and say he has put everyone in danger. Tertullian writes De corona for him and against them, and pushes the question past the crown: whether a man sworn to Christ can be sworn to the standards at all.
stops.quote: more a soldier of God, more steadfast than the rest of his brethren...his head alone uncovered, the useless crown in his hand
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, De corona 1 (ANF tr. S. Thelwall), newadvent.org/fathers/0304.htm
suggested_refs: De corona, on military service and the ceremonial crown

segments.name: Ad Scapulam: the Proconsul and the Darkened Sun

stops.name: Proconsul's residence, Carthage: the letter to Scapula
stops.date_confidence: attested work addressed to Scapula, proconsul of Africa [A, Ad Scapulam 2-3, newadvent.org/fathers/0305.htm]. The date is the conventional one, after the solar eclipse of 14 August 212, per tertullian.org/chronology.htm; the text itself gives no calendar date, and neither the research pool nor the verification pass confirmed the eclipse identification from a primary source.
stops.campa: Scapula is proconsul of Africa and is killing Christians. Tertullian writes to him directly, in the register of a man addressing an official who can still be reasoned with. Then the warning, laid out as precedent: a list of governors who persecuted and what became of them afterward, illness, fire, sudden death. He makes no threat of his own; he describes a pattern. Religion adopted under compulsion is not religion, worship belongs to free will, and a sacrifice extracted by a magistrate is worth nothing to the god who receives it.
stops.quote: It is assuredly no part of religion to compel religion, to which free-will and not force should lead us.
suggested_refs: Ad Scapulam, addressed to the proconsul at Carthage

stops.name: Utica, the sun going out
stops.date_confidence: the passage is attested verbatim [A, Ad Scapulam 3, newadvent.org/fathers/0305.htm]; the association with the solar eclipse of 14 August 212 is a modern astronomical back-calculation and is not stated by Tertullian [R]. The Utica coordinate was corrected during verification to the ancient site at 37.05694 N / 10.06194 E, about 3 km from the pool value.
stops.campa: Forty miles up the coast from Carthage, at Utica, the sun fails. He reports it to Scapula as one item in a docket of warnings and insists on its character: not an ordinary eclipse, since an eclipse arrives when the moon is where the tables say it will be, and this did not. Modern astronomy back-calculates a solar eclipse over Africa on the fourteenth of August, 212, and the date of the whole letter now hangs on that reckoning. What he himself puts on the page is a darkened sky over a provincial town, offered to a proconsul as a thing to be uneasy about. He gives no day, no month and no year.
stops.quote: That sun, too, in the metropolis of Utica, with light all but extinguished, was a portent which could not have occurred from an ordinary eclipse.
suggested_refs: The ancient site of Utica, Africa Proconsularis

stops.name: Carthage, the word trinitas put into Latin
stops.date_confidence: attested text [A, Adversus Praxean 2, ANF tr. Peter Holmes, newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm], conventionally dated after c. 213; Barnes's compressed chronology would end Tertullian's activity around 212, which the standard dating contradicts. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved. The exact slogan una substantia, tres personae does not appear verbatim in this chapter.
stops.campa: Praxeas teaches that Father and Son are one and the same, that the Father himself was born and suffered. Against him Tertullian assembles the vocabulary the Latin West will use for the next fifteen centuries: trinitas, persona, substantia, oeconomia. Three, he says, not in condition but in degree, not in substance but in form, of one substance and one condition and one power. The words that will settle the fourth century are minted in a province, in an argument with one man. Nicaea is more than a century off, and the language still has slack in it, degrees and ranks that the later councils will tighten.
stops.quote: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, Adversus Praxean 2 (ANF tr. Peter Holmes), newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
suggested_refs: Adversus Praxean 2, the earliest major Latin deployment of trinitas

stops.name: Rome, the letter of peace that was recalled
stops.date_confidence: attested report [A, Adversus Praxean 1, newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm]; the events it describes precede Praxeas's intervention and are undated. The unnamed Roman bishop's identity is debated, with Eleutherus and Victor both proposed [R]. The pin is Rome because that is where the events happened; Tertullian is not attested to have been there, and how the news reached him is unrecorded.
stops.campa: He reports what happened at Rome, without ever having been there. A bishop of the city had begun to acknowledge the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca and Maximilla, and had sent letters of peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. Then Praxeas arrived out of Asia with accusations against the prophets and their churches, pressed the authority of the bishop's predecessors, and the letter was withdrawn. Tertullian does not name the bishop; the candidates argued over since are Eleutherus and Victor. What carried this story to Carthage, correspondence or a traveller, is not recorded.
stops.quote: the first to import into Rome from Asia this kind of heretical pravity
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, Adversus Praxean 1 (ANF tr. Peter Holmes), newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
suggested_refs: Adversus Praxean 1, on the recalled letters of peace to Asia and Phrygia

stops.name: Carthage, no flight and no bribe
stops.date_confidence: attested work, dated after c. 213 [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the month orders the segment. Barnes would compress this and the following treatises earlier; the ordering here follows the standard chronology and the contradiction is noted rather than settled.
stops.campa: The question is practical and it divides the congregation: when the soldiers come, may a Christian leave town, or buy his way out with a payment to the officer who would otherwise arrest him. He answers no to both. Persecution does not arrive except by God's will, so evading it is evading God, and the bribe is the worse of the two because it turns the faith into a licensed trade. He is arguing against people who have children, property, and a plausible reading of the gospel that says flee to the next city. The book does not concede them a sentence.
suggested_refs: De fuga in persecutione
sources: Tertullian, De fuga in persecutione, dated after c. 213 at tertullian.org/chronology.htm

stops.name: Carthage, the veil demanded of the unmarried
stops.date_confidence: attested work, in the post-213 cluster [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the month is an ordering device. No specific congregation or individual case is named in the sources available to the research pool.
stops.campa: Married women in the assembly are veiled. Unmarried ones, in Carthage as elsewhere, sit with their heads bare, and he wants that stopped. A virgin is a woman; the custom of the Greek churches is against the local practice; the apostle wrote of women and not of wives. He prosecutes the point with the whole apparatus of a man arguing title in a court, and behind it stands the New Prophecy's demand that discipline tighten rather than slacken as the age runs down. The dispute is over cloth in a room.
suggested_refs: De virginibus velandis, in Corpus Christianorum Series Latina 2

stops.name: Carthage, the concession withdrawn
stops.date_confidence: attested work, in the post-213 cluster [A, tertullian.org/chronology.htm]; the month orders the segment. The hardening against the milder counsel of Ad uxorem is visible in the two texts themselves; whether his wife was still living is unrecorded.
stops.campa: Fifteen or twenty years earlier he had written to his own wife that she should not remarry if he died first, and had allowed that if she did, she should marry only in the Lord. He now withdraws the allowance. A second marriage after a spouse's death is a species of fornication; the Paraclete has closed what the apostle left ajar. The same man, the same doctrine, the same city, and a door that stood open in the first book is nailed shut in the later one. Whether his wife was alive to read it is not recorded anywhere.
stops.quote: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, Ad uxorem II.2 (ANF tr.), newadvent.org/fathers/0404.htm
suggested_refs: De monogamia, read against Ad uxorem

stops.name: Carthage, the edict of the bishop of bishops
stops.date_confidence: attested text [A, De pudicitia 1, newadvent.org/fathers/0407.htm]. The dating is contradictory and is not resolved here: tertullian.org/chronology.htm groups the work with the post-213 treatises, while the research pool cited that same page for 222-223, a reading the verification pass could not confirm; other reference works give 213-223. The target's identity, Callistus of Rome or a Carthaginian bishop, remains unsettled, and it materially affects both the date and the place.
stops.campa: A prelate has issued an edict absolving adultery and fornication after penance, and Tertullian reproduces the wording in order to destroy it. He gives the man two titles, neither of them his: pontifex maximus, which belongs to the emperor's own priesthood, and bishop of bishops. Who was hit by this has never been settled, Callistus at Rome or somebody down the street. The church may forgive such sins in heaven, he argues, and still refuse to seat their doers in the assembly; the power to pardon belongs to the Spirit and to the men who have the Spirit, not to a count of bishops.
stops.quote: I remit, to such as have discharged (the requirements of) repentance, the sins both of adultery and of fornication.
stops.quote_source: Tertullian, De pudicitia 1, quoting the prelate's edict (ANF tr.), newadvent.org/fathers/0407.htm
suggested_refs: De pudicitia 1, and the nineteenth-century argument identifying its target with Callistus
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, noting Monceaux's argument for a Carthaginian bishop

stops.name: Carthage, the prose runs out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The last securely dated work is conventionally placed at 212-213; what follows is arranged by argument rather than evidence [R]. Barnes compresses the whole corpus to end activity around 212, against a traditional dating that extends some works to 222-223. The contradiction stands unresolved in the scholarship and is left standing here.
stops.campa: After the letter to Scapula nothing else in the corpus can be securely dated. The books on discipline follow, in an order scholars arrange by argument rather than by evidence, and then the prose ends. No source records why. He does not sign off, does not announce a last work, does not describe an illness or a journey or a reconciliation. Barnes's reconstruction pulls the whole career in so tight that the life would have to end at this year or one very close to it. The chronology runs out of footholds.
suggested_refs: Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian: A Historical and Literary Study (1971, rev. 1985)

stops.name: Carthage, the presumed place of death
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a weak one. No surviving source records his last residence, health, office, trial, imprisonment or death; the traditional dates c. 220, c. 225 and c. 240 are estimates, not records [R]. Carthage is presumed only because it is his last documented setting. Barnes's proposal of death soon after 212, possibly as a martyr, is supported by no martyr act, cult, tomb or feast.
stops.campa: There is no death date. There is no tomb, no epitaph, no relic, no shrine, no feast day, and no ancient account of how or where he died. Reference works print c. 220, c. 225, c. 240, all of them estimates dressed as records. Barnes has proposed that he died not long after 212 and possibly as a martyr, which no martyr act, no cult and no calendar supports. Jerome, at nearly two centuries' distance, says only that he is reported to have lived to a decrepit old age, and marks the hearsay as hearsay in the saying of it.
stops.quote: is reported to have lived to a decrepit old age
stops.quote_source: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, tr. E. C. Richardson), newadvent.org/fathers/2708.htm
suggested_refs: The absence of any burial, cult or feast day for Tertullian

stops.name: Carthage, give me the master
stops.date_confidence: attested only as Jerome's late report of an oral chain: an elderly Italian named Paul, who claimed to have met a secretary of Cyprian at Rome [A for Jerome's text, R for the anecdote itself]. Cyprian never names Tertullian in any of his own surviving works. The date is Cyprian's episcopate, used to order the segment.
stops.campa: A generation later Cyprian is bishop of this city and, by a story Jerome heard from an old man who had it from Cyprian's own secretary, never let a day pass without reading Tertullian. Cyprian never names him in anything he wrote himself. What he does carry everywhere is the vocabulary: the Latin the schismatic invented becomes the working language of an African church that never gave him a feast day. The story reaches Jerome through three pairs of hands, and in it Cyprian asks for the books by a single phrase. Give me the master.
stops.quote: Give me the master, meaning by this, Tertullian.
stops.quote_source: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, tr. E. C. Richardson), newadvent.org/fathers/2708.htm
suggested_refs: Cyprian's Latin, and the extent of his unacknowledged debt to Tertullian

stops.name: Carthage, the presbyter Jerome describes
stops.date_confidence: attested testimony, written c. 392-393, roughly 170 years after Tertullian's active career [A, Jerome, De viris illustribus 53]. Jerome composed it at Bethlehem; the pin is Tertullian's own city, because the stop is his and not Jerome's. The presbyter claim is in tension with the lay standpoint of Tertullian's own late works, and no African source knows of an ordination. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Almost everything the middle ages knew about the man comes from one paragraph written at Bethlehem, a hundred and seventy years after him, by a scholar working from lists and hearsay. Jerome makes him a presbyter of the African church until middle life, then driven out by the envy of the Roman clergy into the doctrine of Montanus. The difficulty is that the late books speak from among the laity rather than from a pulpit, and no African source knows of any ordination. That sentence has organized every biography since, and there is nothing to check it against.
stops.quote: He was presbyter of the church until middle life, afterwards driven by the envy and abuse of the clergy of the Roman church, he lapsed to the doctrine of Montanus.
stops.quote_source: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, tr. E. C. Richardson), newadvent.org/fathers/2708.htm
suggested_refs: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53, the source of the entire traditional biography
sources: Jerome, De viris illustribus 53, newadvent.org/fathers/2708.htm and tertullian.org/jerome_biog.htm
Timothy D. Barnes, Tertullian, on the unreliability of Jerome's notice

stops.name: Carthage, the Tertullianists give up the basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested testimony written c. 428, two centuries after Tertullian [A, Augustine, De haeresibus 86]. Augustine gives no dates for Tertullian's own break, and his claim that Tertullian separated even from the Montanists and founded his own congregations is uncorroborated by any earlier source [R].
stops.campa: Two centuries after his death a congregation at Carthage still carries his name, and it has dwindled to almost nothing. Augustine, bishop of Hippo up the coast, records the end of it: the last Tertullianists come over to Catholic communion and hand across their basilica. He also reports what he takes to have happened at the start, that Tertullian broke from the church over Cataphrygian teaching, condemning second marriage as debauchery, then broke from the Montanists too and gathered his own people. No earlier source says any such thing. The basilica changed hands, and that much is documented.
suggested_refs: Augustine, De haeresibus 86, on the Tertullianistae of Carthage

stops.name: Paris, the Codex Agobardinus
stops.date_confidence: attested manuscript, ninth century, 204 folios [A, tertullian.org/manuscripts/agobardinus.htm]. That page dates Agobard 814-840; he in fact succeeded to Lyon in 816, and 814 reflects a disputed earlier designation as coadjutor. The pin is the BnF Richelieu site, where the manuscript department holds Latin 1622.
stops.campa: The oldest surviving book of his works is a ninth-century parchment of two hundred and four leaves, copied for Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, and given by him to the cathedral of Saint Stephen there. It is water-damaged, missing its last leaves, and breaks off in the middle of De carne Christi. For several texts it is the only witness there is, and for one of them the only manuscript that carries the title. It sits now in the manuscript department of the Bibliotheque nationale de France as Latin 1622. Four other families of copies stand behind the printed corpus, and one of them, the Corbie group, is itself lost.
suggested_refs: Paris, BnF Ms. Latin 1622, digitized at iiif.biblissima.fr
sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertullian, on the five manuscript families

stops.name: Basel, the corpus printed whole
stops.date_confidence: attested [A, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatus_Rhenanus, for the 1521 editio princeps at Basel; tertullian.org/rediscovery.htm for Poggio's find of 1416-17, Niccoli's Apologeticum of 1424, Benalio's Venice printing before 1493 and Scinzenzeler's Milan printing of 1494]. Day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: Poggio Bracciolini turns up a manuscript around Saint Gall in 1416 or 1417; Niccolo Niccoli acquires a copy of the Apologeticum in 1424 and Ambrogio Traversari transcribes it; before 1493 Bernardino Benalio prints that one treatise at Venice, and Ulrich Scinzenzeler prints it again at Milan the year after. Everything else waits, in a handful of damaged codices, for another quarter of a century. In 1521 at Basel, Beatus Rhenanus brings out the first printed edition of the works together.
suggested_refs: Beatus Rhenanus, ed., Opera Q. Septimii Florentis Tertulliani (Basel, 1521)

stops.name: Paris, a face invented in 1584
stops.date_confidence: attested [A, the 1584 engraving in Andre Thevet, Les Vrais Pourtraits et Vies des Hommes Illustres]. The characterization of it as a later representation rather than contemporary evidence is the research pool's own gloss and was wrongly presented as a Wikipedia quotation; the verification pass caught that and it is not quoted here. The four-part name Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus is a medieval manuscript-title tradition, attested in no inscription [R].
stops.campa: Andre Thevet engraves him for a gallery of illustrious men, a bearded head in a scholar's frame, and it becomes the face reproduced ever since. It is made thirteen hundred years after the death of a man nobody described. No ancient portrait exists, no statue, no physical detail in any source, nothing to compare the engraving against and nothing to correct it with. Even the four-part name printed under such images, Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus, comes from the titles of medieval manuscripts rather than from any stone. What survives is entirely words.
suggested_refs: Andre Thevet, Les Vrais Pourtraits et Vies des Hommes Illustres (Paris, 1584)
